verification: Every PMID resolved through NCBI E-utilities esummary (title, first author, journal, year compared) and abstracts read through efetch; trial sponsors through the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API; FDA pages and PDFs (503A category list of 14 May 2026, Category 2 page, October 2024 advisory-committee minutes, warning letter), DailyMed labels (SPL XML), Drugs@FDA and openFDA, the Federal Register API, eCFR and uscode.house.gov fetched live on 2026-09-24 and read; open-access full text via Europe PMC (Giustina 2024, Dominikowski 2026); the Endocrine Society guideline's recommendations read on the publisher's page. Nothing is included on the strength of a guide reference alone.
grader: Graded 2026-09-24 by the agent under Omar Saleem's delegation ("you should be able to do that from the guide"); rule set below; final review Dr. Hannah-Shmouni
gradingRule: Grade = certainty the source gives for the specific clinical statement the lesson makes, on the guides' A–D scale. A: consistent large RCTs or approval-grade evidence. B: at least one well-designed, adequately powered RCT or an independent, quality-stratified meta-analysis (either direction). C: small or sponsor-funded RCTs without independent replication, or pooled trials dominated by them. D: animal, in-vitro, mechanistic, case series, manufacturer dossiers. 'context' = history, reviews used for framing, trial registrations without results, analytical or regulatory records (regulatory records are primary for status statements, not graded for efficacy). Where the two guides disagree, the lesson states both and the claim takes the grade the primary evidence supports. Observational studies (added 2026-09-24, GRADE starting point, for the final reviewer to confirm): adequately sized cohort, case-control or cross-sectional studies grade C for the association they measured; small or single-centre ones grade D; any causal claim drawn from observational data grades D. Meta-analyses of observational studies grade at most B, and only for association. Guidelines and consensus statements are 'context', cited for what they recommend, not graded as evidence.

claims.text: Growth hormone acts mainly in the dermis: its receptor is expressed more by dermal fibroblasts than keratinocytes, and GH increases fibroblast numbers and supports collagen synthesis. IGF-1, made locally by fibroblasts and melanocytes, acts on keratinocytes through the IGF-1 receptor; in culture IGF-1, not GH, drives keratinocyte proliferation.
claims.reviewNote: mechanism only; taught as the mechanism register
claims.gradeDecision: D — in vitro and mechanism review

claims.text: Human hair follicles operate a functional peripheral equivalent of the somatotropic (GHRH–GH–IGF-1) axis ex vivo.
GH secretion and IGF-1 decline progressively with age (the somatopause); IGF-1 must be read against age- and sex-adjusted ranges, so a value low for a young adult is often normal for age.
claims.reviewNote: physiology; the interpretation point is the guide's own testing advice

claims.text: Human skin reflects the axis at its extremes: adults with GH deficiency have a thinner epidermis and reduced sweating on biopsy, not fully reversed by treatment of childhood-onset deficiency; in acromegaly, dermal glycosaminoglycan deposition and oedema thicken and puff the skin of the face, hands and feet.
claims.reviewNote: disease-state observations; they show what deficiency and excess do, and nothing about cosmetic benefit
claims.gradeDecision: C — small observational study plus clinical review

claims.text: In people with burns over 40% of body surface, recombinant GH shortened burn-wound and donor-site healing in pooled small randomized trials (13 RCTs, 701 people), with more hyperglycaemia; the evidence carries risk of bias.
claims.reviewNote: the only clinical skin setting with randomized evidence for GH
claims.gradeDecision: C — pooled small RCTs, independent review

claims.text: A much-cited 1990 NEJM study gave GH to 12 healthy men over 60 with nine untreated men as comparison and no placebo; skin thickness rose 7.1% (P = 0.07, not significant). A 1996 RCT in 28 older men found 15% more collagen deposited in implanted wound tubes on GH — a laboratory surrogate.
claims.reviewNote: numbers read from the abstracts; doses not reproduced
claims.gradeDecision: D (Rudman) · C (Papadakis) — no visible skin outcome in healthy adults

claims.text: In healthy older adults, randomized trials of GH show small body-composition changes (about 2 kg less fat, 2 kg more lean mass) with more oedema, arthralgia, carpal tunnel syndrome and gynaecomastia and a trend to diabetes, while strength and endurance change little; GH is not recommended as anti-ageing therapy. A&RE grades this advice A; on the course rule the trials give B, with the same conclusion.
claims.reviewNote: guide A vs course B named in the lesson and sent to the author
claims.gradeDecision: B — independent systematic review plus an independent RCT

claims.text: In the US (21 U.S.C. 333(e), current text read September 2026), knowingly distributing human growth hormone for any use other than treating a disease or recognized condition authorised by FDA, on a physician's order, is a federal offence.

claims.text: Tesamorelin, a GHRH analogue, reduced visceral fat by about 15% versus placebo at 26 weeks in two developer-run phase 3 RCTs (806 patients pooled), with subcutaneous fat unchanged; in the US it has been FDA-approved since 2010 for reduction of excess abdominal fat in HIV-infected adults with lipodystrophy, and its label excludes weight loss. Both guides grade it A — for that indication only.
claims.gradeDecision: A — two consistent phase 3 RCTs; approval-grade for this indication

claims.text: Tesamorelin's label reports IGF-1 above +2 SDS in 47% (above +3 SDS in 36%) of treated patients at 26 weeks, states that the effects of prolonged IGF-1 elevation are unknown, reports diabetes-range HbA1c in 5% vs 1% on placebo, lists fluid retention, and contraindicates use in active malignancy.
claims.reviewNote: label figures from the pivotal trials; the course states them as safety facts and never as targets

claims.text: A PubMed search in September 2026 found no randomized trial with a skin outcome for tesamorelin, CJC-1295, ipamorelin or IGF-1 LR3; the closest human skin data for a GHRH analogue are a 1997 single-blind study of [Nle27]GHRH(1-29) in 19 older adults, with caliper skin thickness rising after a placebo lead-in and no parallel control.
claims.reviewNote: search: agent name AND skin terms AND (randomized controlled trial[pt] OR clinical trial[pt]), 24 Sep 2026
claims.gradeDecision: D — absence of trials; one tiny uncontrolled study

claims.text: CJC-1295 with DAC raised GH and IGF-1 for days in phase 1 trials in healthy adults, with no clinical endpoint; CJC-1295 without DAC ('Mod GRF 1-29') and IGF-1 LR3 have no peer-reviewed human studies. The Hormonaly guides rate CJC-1295/ipamorelin C ('anecdotal'); on the course rule the evidence for any clinical or skin benefit is D.
claims.reviewNote: grade disagreement named in the lesson and sent to the author
claims.gradeDecision: D — pharmacodynamics or nothing; guides say C

claims.text: Ipamorelin's only efficacy RCT (postoperative ileus, phase 2) showed no benefit over placebo; ibutamoren (MK-677) raised GH, IGF-1 and fat-free mass in a 2-year RCT in older adults without improving strength or function, raised fasting glucose and lowered insulin sensitivity, and a hip-fracture phase IIb trial was stopped early for a heart-failure signal.
claims.reviewNote: raised hormone levels did not translate into clinical benefit
claims.gradeDecision: C — small RCTs, negative or harm-signalling

claims.text: In the US, sermorelin was approved as Geref (1990, diagnostic; 1997, idiopathic GH deficiency in children), discontinued in 2008, and its approvals withdrawn in 2009 at the maker's request; FDA determined in 2013 that this was not for safety or effectiveness reasons. As of 24 September 2026 no sermorelin product is marketed (Drugs@FDA), and sermorelin appears in no 503A category (FDA list of 14 May 2026).
claims.reviewNote: the legal basis on which pharmacies compound sermorelin is not settled by any FDA document found; flagged to the author, not taught

claims.text: US compounding status (FDA 503A category list of 14 May 2026; Category 2 page current 22 April 2026; 21 CFR 216.23 as of September 2026): no GH-axis peptide is on the 503A bulks list; ibutamoren is in 503A and 503B Category 2; GHRP-2 and GHRP-6 are in 503A Category 3 and 503B Category 2; CJC-1295 and ipamorelin are listed among withdrawn Category 2 nominations, with ipamorelin still in 503B Category 2; FDA's advisory committee voted against ibutamoren (1–13) and ipamorelin (0–12, 1 abstention) in October 2024; a 2020 warning letter named CJC 1295, ipamorelin, IGF1-LR3, GHRP-2, GHRP-6 and MK 677 as ineligible for 503A exemptions.
claims.reviewNote: A&RE's 'Cat. 2' for CJC-1295/ipamorelin is out of date; corrected here and sent to the author

claims.text: Skin and soft-tissue signs of GH excess include puffiness and thickening of the face, hands and feet from glycosaminoglycan deposition and oedema, oily skin with large pores, hyperhidrosis, skin tags and acanthosis nigricans, with slow acral and jaw enlargement; the Endocrine Society recommends IGF-1 measurement for typical acral and facial features and suggests it when several associated conditions cluster (sleep apnoea, type 2 diabetes, debilitating arthritis, carpal tunnel syndrome, hyperhidrosis, hypertension).

GH-axis drugs commonly cause fluid retention (oedema, arthralgia, paraesthesia, carpal tunnel symptoms), usually transient and dose-related, and glucose intolerance; somatropin labelling asks that pre-existing nevi be monitored for growth or malignant change.

Observed human data on IGF-1 and cancer are associations: higher circulating IGF-1 is linked with modestly higher risks of prostate, breast, colorectal and thyroid cancer, with reverse causation not excluded; acromegaly shows a slightly raised cancer incidence in pooled studies (SIR 1.5) that a nationwide cohort did not confirm (SIR 1.1).
claims.reviewNote: kept separate from mechanism and from treatment cohorts

claims.text: GH treatment cohorts are largely reassuring for replacement: no clear raised cancer risk in 23,984 GH-treated children with growth failure and no other major disease, and a 2022 consensus found no association between GH replacement and primary tumour or recurrence; people with GH-receptor deficiency have very little cancer. No long-term cancer data exist for secretagogues or IGF-1 LR3 used for ageing or skin — the mitogenic risk there is plausible and unmeasured.
claims.reviewNote: treatment cohorts describe replacement in deficiency and do not transfer to supraphysiological use
claims.gradeDecision: C — observational; open question stated as such

authorFindings: A&RE ch.15 table ('CJC-1295 / ipamorelin … Cat. 2 (not in 2026 review)') and the drug-safety page ('503A Category-2'): FDA's Category 2 page (content current 22 April 2026) lists CJC-1295 and ipamorelin among Category 2 nominations that were withdrawn (ipamorelin remains in 503B Category 2), and neither appears in FDA's 503A category list of 14 May 2026. Suggest re-dating the status.

Grade disagreement — A&RE rates CJC-1295/ipamorelin 'GRADE C anecdotal' and the Pocket Guide rates CJC-1295 and ipamorelin C; by the Pocket Guide's own scale 'anecdotal' is D. Their human data are phase 1 hormone-level studies (CJC-1295 with DAC), one negative phase 2 trial (ipamorelin, postoperative ileus) and nothing for CJC-1295 without DAC. The course teaches D for any clinical or skin benefit and names the disagreement.

A&RE ch.14 — 'illegal to prescribe for anti-aging in the US GRADE A' attaches an evidence grade to a legal statement. The statute (21 U.S.C. 333(e)) prohibits knowing distribution for unauthorised uses; the trial evidence (Liu 2007: 18 small RCT populations, 220 treated) grades B on the course rule. The conclusion — GH is not an anti-ageing therapy — is unchanged.
PPG CJC-1295 entry — 'Teichman et al. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2005;91:799-805' is 2006 (March; epub December 2005), PMID 16352683.

PPG IGF-1 LR3 entry — 'Dominikowski A et al. Peptides marketed for performance and longevity: absence of human studies. 2025 (PMID 42395176)': the PMID resolves to Dominikowski A et al., 'The emerging landscape of performance-enhancing peptides modulating GH-IGF1 axis…', Front Endocrinol 2026;17:1822475 — the title and year differ.

PPG CJC-1295 entry — the 'fatal event in a CJC-1131 trial' within 'related long-acting GHRH-analogue programs': PubMed describes CJC-1131 as a long-acting GLP-1 analogue (Léger 2004, PMID 15357960; Tiessen 2008, PMID 18793574), and no fatal event could be located. The course uses FDA's own summary of CJC-1295 adverse events (increased heart rate, systemic vasodilatory reaction) instead.

PPG sermorelin regulatory line is garbled ('not on not categorized on FDA's 14 May 2026 roster restricted list'). Verified: sermorelin appears in no 503A category (14 May 2026); Geref's approvals were withdrawn in 2009 at the maker's request and FDA's 2013 determination found no safety or effectiveness reason. No FDA document found states the legal basis on which 503A pharmacies compound sermorelin today; the course states only the verified facts and suggests the author address this.

PPG adverse-effects section (pp. 119–120, 'IGF-1 targets' and dose reduction) is titration guidance and stays outside the source lock; module 06 uses only the recognition and referral content. Precision note: the label's figure is IGF-1 above +2 SDS in 47% at 26 weeks (the guide says 'exceeded ULN').
The brief's verification request — Falutz J et al., N Engl J Med 2007;357:2359–70 — resolves to PMID 18057338 (title, first author, journal and year match); A&RE ch.15 ref 2 is correct.

Not in either guide, worth adding — Rudman 1990 (much cited; its skin result missed significance), Lange 2001 (skin in GH deficiency and acromegaly), the 2014 Cochrane review of GH in major burns (the only skin indication with RCTs), Khorram 1997 (the only GHRH-analogue study with a skin outcome), Nass 2008 and Adunsky 2011 (ibutamoren: IGF-1 up, no functional benefit, heart-failure signal), FDA's October 2024 advisory-committee votes on ipamorelin and ibutamoren, the Egrifta label's IGF-1 figures and the somatropin label's nevus-monitoring warning, and the IGF-1 cancer epidemiology (Renehan 2004, Knuppel 2020, Dal 2018, SAGhE 2017).
